samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert W. Schoning was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: [Note: speakers do not clearly identify themselves] The day is 22 November, 2003, from Corvallis, Oregon. The name of our veteran is Robert W. Schoning. Veteran’s birthday is 9-20-1923. Current address, 1775 Northwest Arbol Place, Corvallis, Oregon, 97330. Name of interviewers: Brandon Lemke, Leslie Curry, Amanda Wilson and Josh...

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Singsas.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Singsas. Our organization is Arnold Air Society of Air Force ROTC.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Okay. Our first question, sir, is, were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: I enlisted. I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: You enlisted? Okay. Where were you living at the time when you were enlisted?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Seattle, Washington.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Seattle? Why did you join?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Oh, World War II started (laughter).

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: And -- yeah?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: We were going to be drafted.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yah?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: They were calling everybody in my age group.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Why did you choose the Marine Corps?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Oh, I, uh, wanted to fight (laughter). My dad had been a marine in World War II, and I had just had an affinity to the Marine Corps. I just wanted to be a marine.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: I’m kind of curious. Okay, for officers, we go through field training, but you went through a boot camp right? What kind of, like -

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: We went through boot camp before I went through officer training.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: And what kind of experiences and everything did you have with that?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Oh, typical boot camp, all the things you’ve heard about. It’s difficult program and if you’re in good shape physically, it’s not a problem; and I was, and so it wasn’t a problem for me.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Okay. You said that you served in World War II in Korea. Do you have any things that your units did or anything that you’d like to comment about that, like what your mission was?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Well, I, the most significant time was in Korea where I had -- when I first got there in September of 1950. I had a machine gun platoon, and then later I had a rifle platoon. And then later I was with the Battalion Plants Operations staff, DS3. That was the most significant time.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: You mentioned earlier that you had a few awards and medals awarded to you. Can you comment further on those for us?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh, they were, I got them when I had -- when we were in combat in Korea, in 1950 and ‘51.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Do you mind sharing with us, maybe, some of the most memorable things that you did when you were overseas, like in -

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Let me - I had prepared some text --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: For something totally different.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: About my church and my faith, and they asked me to comment on it, so I wrote some things.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That’d be great.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: And I’ll read a couple paragraphs that relate to it, kind of the point you said.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: (Reading) "I stayed in the active reserve, Marine Corps reserve, and in August of 1950, I was recalled to active duty for 19 months and spent a year of in Korea. That year, on active duty in the Marine Corps, much of it in combat conditions, was from some stand points the most significant period of my life. I would never be the same afterwards. I learned much about myself under widely varying circumstances -- what I was willing to do and not to do and why, when I was afraid and when I wasn’t, why I was afraid and why I wasn’t, when to lead and when to follow, when do delegate, how to delegate, when to provide leadership and when to encourage leadership, how to be disciplined and how to admitteth?? through discipline. After being involved in a variety of circumstanced some developed the feeling that the Lord would take you when it’s time and until then, do your job without undo concern. That philosophy of partnership with the Lord works in many places and situations. When I left Korea in September of 51’, I had an inner calm and satisfaction of who I was and what I could do, if necessary. For the confidence, it gave me self-assurance, which served me well in all my subsequent activities, both in my remaining years in the reserve and by my hand in my varied civilian activities. I doubt that I could have or would have acquired that feeling under any other circumstances. I am forever thankful for that experience, for having it, for surviving it, for the countless benefits resulting from it in subsequent years. I am not sure what the role God for me in that year in Korea. Yes, I prayed to Him often. Many times, I was in a position where I could have been injured or killed by enemy action. I wasn’t but people near me were. Did I believe more in God more than they did? I don’t think that was why I survived and they didn’t. We may have had the same philosophy about, when it’s time, you will go, irrespective of what you do or are doing. Maybe it was their time and not mine. Maybe God had a special mission, later mission, for me and He didn’t have one for them. Or maybe their mission was simply more pressing than mine. Maybe I was just luckier at the time than they were and I would simply have to wait longer to be with God and under different circumstances. After a given period of time in Korea, I didn’t focus as much on what I had to do to stay alive as I did on what I needed to do to fulfill my responsibilities as a platoon leader. Unrelated to whether I would or wouldn’t be killed, my faith gave me some peace of mind to function effectively, to concentrate on what had to be done, when and how. With additional experience comes satisfaction and confidence. Faith builds and helps achieve success. That’s not to say that I was always successful in what I did. I was not. But I continually learned from the mistakes, advice from others, and why when things did not go well. There are different kinds of ways to define faith: Faith in God, faith in yourself, faith in your fellow man, faith in country, faith in beliefs, faith in fate, what we will be or -- what will be will be. It can be related in different ways or unrelated depending on the individual. I believe in God, that He loves me and is looking for me as part of a bigger plan. In the process, He has helped me gain faith in myself to be a better person, to accomplish certain things, to believe in and follow the commandments." That’s about the end of it.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Thank you, sir.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Okay. Now, ___.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: I’m just kind of curious about all the details, I guess. What did you guys do on your leave time when you were over in China and, just, kind of things that you’d -- everyday stuff.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: When I was in China, the war was over. We were on our ship going overseas, presumably to land in China -- or Japan, and fight the war in Japan. We were in the middle of the ocean when V-J Day came, which was victory over Japan, and so, then there was no landing in Japan, so we came to China. And there was a stab of Japanese military there. And we, I was in the Service Battalion in the 6th Marine Division, and we repatriated Japanese soldiers during that year I was there. And then, I came back and was in the reserve and then we got called up in Korea, and went there, and I had, it was what I said, the most valuable time in my life, being in combat with the Marines. And I was up at the Chosin Reservoir, and then came back, and it was in difficult circumstances, very cold. It was 20 below or more, and that’s when the Chinese people didn’t expect the Chinese, and they came in. There were a hundred thousand Chinese. The famous quote of General Puller who was commanding, the general of the 1st Marine Regiment, he said that the Chinese had come in and surrounded us and we decided to leave the Reservoir and get back. He said, "They’ve got us surrounded. Now the bastards won’t get away." (Laughter) And that was the kind of philosophy that he had. That was a critical time for, 8 or 10 days, whatever it was, when we were coming back South. And then we, later after we got, went South, and got reinforced and went back up and spent a year, total year, fighting the Chinese and the North Koreans.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: I have a question for you, sir. You said your father was in the Marine Corps.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Marine Corps in World War I.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: And you decided to enlist because of the interaction you had with him and the kind of respect you had with the Corps.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Yeah; exactly.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: When you came out of the boot camp, and you were actually on active duty, and you were deployed over into China, what was your feelings, like, from what you expected, and what you actually experienced during your time in the service?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Well, let me clarify a couple things. One, when I enlisted in October, ’42, it was with the understanding that it was in a D12 program. I was in college at the time, and the program was that we knew that we’d go to boot camp. We got through boot camp, we’d go to officer school. And if we made it, we’d be an officer. If we didn’t, we’d have to stay until the war was over. And so, after boot camp, I went to some advanced training for 22 weeks and then went to officer school. Oh and we’re there, for, I don’t know, 16 weeks, maybe. And then went to Camp Pendleton and then went overseas and we expected to land in Japan and fight and that was before the President dropped the atomic bomb. But then of course, it was a tremendous relief to us. There would have been huge losses, both of our people and their people if we had had to land. And so it was a great relief to know that we weren’t gonna have to fight in Japan on the mainland at the camp. And, so anyway, and it was just an experience to be in Marine Corps knowing that we had the job to do, but it wasn’t going to be in combat over there, and it wasn’t.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: What was your, what was your primary job, I guess your mission while you were over there?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Oh, I was, I was Battalion Recreation officer and I was also Graves Registration Platoon officer, and I think that was, those were the duties. And then I had other additional duties of various kind, but that was basically it; and we were in, because I was in the Service Battalion, it was a service function and there was no combat or nothing associated with that. It was strictly, totally peacetime for us. Now, there some people elsewhere in China that had a little different functions and had some problems, combat-wise, but we did not; so it was kind of like peacetime Marine Corps. And you asked what I did when I had time off? I played golf. There was a lovely golf course; and it was a lovely beach. It was Tsingtau, is where I was. It was, for years it had been the headquarters for the Pacific Fleet. And they had maneuvers there every year, the Navy did. And so it was an international settlement for many countries. The people of many countries did represent it. It was good real estate, as far as I was concerned.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Do you feel that the stuff that you experienced while you were in service pulled you closer to your fellow soldiers and officers and stuff like that?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: When you’re in the Marine Corps, it is that way. Once a Marine, always a Marine, and you have a tremendous feeling of support. Rely on people. They rely on you. And it’s an experience you’ll never get over, and particularly having been in combat with them. It’s, as I mentioned in the text, it gives you confidence and the feeling of self-assurance. In my judgment, you can’t get it any other way. Or at least, it’s a wonderful way to get it.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Have you joined any veterans’ organizations after, since you’ve been out of the Marines?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: I belong to the Retired Officers Association, have, for many years. As a matter of fact, I’m a lifetime member. And they recently changed the name from, it used to be TROA, The Retired Officers Association and it’s now called Military Officers Association of America. The change was this past year and the thrust was, to let people know that it wasn’t just for the retired officers. It was for any officers; and so to belong, you have to serve one day as a commissioned officer in any branch of service, any of the seven branches of service. So, yes, and I’ve been active in that, we have a club here in Oregon. Nationwide, there’s about 380,000 members; and in Oregon, there’s about 1200 members and there are eight chapters and I belong to one of the chapters here and I’ve been very active in that chapter, for years.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: I was also curious about what your career was after you retired from the Marines or what you did afterwards.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: I was a fishery biologist to start with. I got a degree in fishery from the University of Washington and then worked with the Oregon Fish Commission until I was called to Active Duty and then was away and then came back. And so I spent 24 years with the Oregon Fish Commission. The last 11, I was director. And then I got an offer to go to Washington DC to work with the National Marine Fisheries Service as a deputy director of the National Service. I was that for a year and a half and then I became a director of that for five and a half years. And that was, from a fishery standpoint, that was a very significant part of my life. It was, at that time we passed the 200-Mile Fisheries Act, which was the most significant fisheries legislation in the 200-year history of our country and our agency had responsibility through implementing it. We played a major role in drafting the legislation and then implementing it. And I was director, and we implemented it. So, it was very satisfying from an informational standpoint. And then I worked with them and retired after a total of 20 years with the federal government. And 24 years I was a state O and M after I was with the director in Washington, I came out and I was a professor at the university here at Oregon State (laughter).

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Do you feel that your experiences in the Military kinda helped you along that, your life success?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Kinda helped me along (laughter)? Yeah, there are some. It was the most important part of my life, particularly the year in combat.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: You mentioned that it was the most important aspect of your life. As future officers, could you kind of comment on some of the significant events, maybe start with when you first became an officer and kind of progress through your distinguished career, kind of what you experienced along the route from 2nd Lieutenant to the rank of Colonel, when you retired? A Well, it’d have to be, after coming back from the Service, from active duty in China, I joined the Reserve unit as a 1st battalion, and I just stayed active. We had, at that time, it was one weekend a month, Tuesday nights, and we’d to go two weeks in summer camp. So I continued in that program, and then we got called up for Korea. I was a 1st Lieutenant, then left, came back after 19 months, active duty, and then joined the Reserve, rejoined the unit. And I just gradually got promoted, and more responsibility, and finally I had, I was a Battalion commander in Portland and ran the Battalion for a couple years and then we took them to summer camp and trained them. It was a heck of an experience. And there’s no question in my mind whatever that the time in Korea made a huge difference, showed me what I could do, could and couldn’t do, and expected to do as a leader, and run the troops, and the Battalion got very high ratings from the district. And then a while, I was Battalion commander right after I finished my tour as Battalion commander. You can only have it for a couple years, and I think I got one extension. My former Battalion commander in Korea, at that time he was a colonel and I was a 1st lieutenant. He stayed and he was a regular, and then when I finished my time in the Battalion, I was a colonel and he was a colonel. And we were good friends and so he developed a program called Camp High Sierra. And he asked me to run it. And what it was, it was a program between the business community of San Francisco, the Marine Corps, and the police department of San Francisco. And the program was to take a hundred kids a week for six weeks, bring them up to a camp up in the high sierra mountains of California and show em’ somebody cared about them. And the business community provided the money, the Marine Corps ran it, and the police department chose the kids. And so we brought a hundred kids a week up. And did lots of things. We fished, played in the snow, bivouacked up in the mountains, did all kinds of competition, taught them to clean their barracks, whatever. And it was a very satisfying experience. And I ran that camp for two years. Six weeks I’d go down. For six weeks I got leave from my job. And we had some of the Reserve, or some of the regular Marines from our Reserve unit as staff. And so we had, I forgot, about eight or ten Marines. And they ran it. It was a wonderful experience for these kids. The kids would come off the streets of San Francisco. As I remember, about a third of them had run-ins with the police of various kinds. They were eight to fourteen years old. And, it was a wonderful experience (pause). See, and then I had to get out. After the, you can only have the Battalion for so long. And then I came back to Washington DC and I just dropped out of the program. I got with my other civilian duties, I no longer went to drills, and then I had to retire.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Well, I was wondering if you had any words of advice for us being future officers?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Join the Marines (laughter). Is it too late (laughter)? You don’t want to be in the best outfit (laughter)?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Her boyfriend did (laughter).

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah, my boyfriend did (laughter).

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Okay, yeah. There was something about you I liked (laughter). I was trying to figure out what it is (laughter). That’s what it is (laughter). Now, what’s your other question? What was your question, really?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Words of advice for future officers, sir.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: (Pause) Believe in it, first of all. Believe in what you’re doing. You have to do that. If you don’t, it’s, you’re wasting your time and you’re wasting the government’s money and the government’s time. And it’s not fair to the people who are going to serve under you. You have to believe in it and you have to do the best you can. And you have to look for ways to do things better. Don’t feel that you’ve got the only right answers. There’s, I recently heard a very impressive inspirational speaker, who was a retired air force colonel, Colonel Hubbard, who, as part of his speech said, "Every time I give," and he had given his speech over 10,000 times in 53 countries of the world. He was a prisoner of war for six and a half years in Vietnam. Anyway, one of the points he made was, he said, "When I give a talk, after I’m finish finished, I pass out Post It notes to everybody in the audience; and I tell them, ‘anybody who’s ever done anything you that you couldn’t have done better, write it on this note and give it to me.’" And he said, "I’ve had two notes in all the talks I’ve given. One was, a woman said, ‘I had my son John.’" And he says, "You’re right. I’m not gonna go on that." "Another one," he said, "the only other one I got said, ‘I married Frank.’" And he responded, and he said, "I met Frank, and you could have done better." And so anyway, the whole point is that, is never, in my judgment, there’s never anything you’re doing that you can’t do better. And so don’t feel that you’re the authority on it. Seek input from anybody anytime. You should not care what the source is. You should consider what the substance is. And look for that, and say, well, how can we do this better? And if you can get ideas from somebody else, include them, and they will be supported, you will be supported, you’ll have a better result, and it’ll be satisfying to everybody.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Well, is there anything else that we haven’t covered in the interview that you’d like to add?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: I don’t, I don’t know of anything else at the moment (pause), but obviously do the best you can. It’s so important. I’ve encountered people in the Service, various branches of the service, who felt the Government owed them a living or, tried to get by with less than their best, and it’s, a terrible mistake and a, bad error in judgment when they have that kind of philosophy, totally a disservice to the people under you, and the people will recognize that when you are an officer and have people serving under you. They’ll recognize that. And you don’t want that.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: I guess, throughout your career, what gave you the confidence to get through both the good times and the bad times?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Well, I guess good upbringing by my parents; and I have a brother who was a colonel officer in the Air Force. He retired as a two-star general, and he had the same basic philosophy, do the best you can, anytime you can. Help people and (pause), maybe that’s -- repeat the question again?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: You mentioned that, as a future officer, one of the best things we can do is just be confident, that we can always do better. So how would you build that confidence?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: By doing things, seeking responsibility. There’s, this is the philosophy I’ve had when I’d been a supervisor for a long time. And that is that, when somebody gives you a job, too many times I’ve found people that say, "Well, that’s not my job" or, "I don‘t have time" or, "I’m full with all the other things I’ve got to do." You always want to, when your boss gives you an assignment, regardless of whether it’s your, in your job description or anything else, welcome it. He could be giving you that assignment for several reasons. One, he wants to see how good you are at it. Second, he wants to see your attitude. Third, he may consider you for promotion. He wants to see if you’re willing to take on additional responsibilities, or if you just make excuses. And so, whenever you get an opportunity, seek for it. And even though they used to for years -- say, maybe they still do, I don’t know, in the Military, "You don’t ever volunteer. You always just wait until you have to do it." Don’t do that. Volunteer for things because, if you want to get ahead, that’s the way to get ahead. You do the things you’re supposed to, plus, you do the things that, or more than just what you’re supposed to do. And then somebody will take notice and say, "Yeah, look at that, that wasn’t his assignment or her assignment, and look how well she handled it? She took it willingly. The only question she asked me was, ‘When do you want it done?’" And so you do that. And people recognize that quick and give you more responsibility. Now, you do that with the understanding that you’re going to welcome responsibility. You want more of it cause’ you can handle it, and you want a promotion, you want more, other aspects of that. And if you don’t want that, then, obviously, you don’t do that. But, presumably, in the Service, you want to get ahead, you want to get promoted, you want to serve your country and do the job right. Well, then, look for opportunities to do that. There are a number of times, I’ve had, one classic example as far as I’m concerned, when I was in Fisheries in Washington, the passing 200-mile Fisheries Act. There was a real problem. Our fishermen were being out-fished by foreign vessels by some 2500 foreign vessels fishing off the coast at the time and taking, three and a half million metric tons of fish every year. And we had to do something about. So Congress passed a law in March, or in April of 1976, and it was to be effective January 1st, or March 1st of 1977. We looked at it, our agency, we had responsibility for it, and said, "Ya’ can’t do, what you’ve told us to do in this law, in the time you gave us. We have to do it." So we went, we figured out what you had to do and there about four or five things. You had to change the law that was passed but hadn’t been implemented yet. So we basically went to Congress and said, "We can’t do what you’ve passed, and we’ll have egg on our face because we’ll have to stop all the foreign nations from fishing in our waters because of the things you’ve said in this law. So we’ll give you some suggested changes between now and the implementation date, and if you do those, we can make it work." And people said, "Oh, you can’t do that. How can you tell Congress that they passed a law that you can’t even enforce yet, on time?" And so, we did. We passed it. We sent it to the House. We worked with the staff at the time, drafted some text, a couple one-liners, or two sentences in three or four cases, and the House suspended the rules on the floor of the House of Representatives, passed it, sent it to the Senate the next day. They suspended the rules on the floor of the Senate, passed it the next day, sent it to the President, and it became law, and it was implemented. And we had no egg on the face and it worked. People said, "You can’t do that. No way is Congress gonna say, ‘We’re gonna -- we’ll change the law before you even try to implement it.’" But it worked. So anyway, that’s my example of "Don’t be deterred." You’ll be surprised what you can accomplish. Okay. Any other questions?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: I had one more question, but, would you like some water at all?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Okay. You mentioned -

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Water isn’t gonna solve my problems (laughter).

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: I mentioned, or you mentioned rather, that you should search out responsibilities and opportunities. What were some, probably the top three that you sought out, that you remember really impacted your life?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: (Pause) Oh, one was when I was with the Fish Commission, I was the director of research. And the person came in to run the organization, who was, would be, or was my immediate boss, had come from Washington DC, and he wanted to do other things really than run the agency, and he wanted to leave that with somebody else, so he said, "I’d like to have you take the job." And I’d just become director of research. And we were out of Clackamas, Oregon. It was with other biologists and it was a great life for us. And we liked the community we lived in. We liked the work and everything. And I said, "What if I don’t take it? Who will get it?" And he said, "Well, here’s the list of about eight people. One of those people will get it." And I looked at it and I said, "I’m better than any of those eight. And my answer is yes, I’ll take it." And so I took it. And in some respects, I would have preferred to be there, but, in Clackamas still and not got to Portland, where the headquarters were, and so I went there. And then, in a year and a half, they fired him and I became director. And it was tremendously satisfying to me; and, as a matter of fact, we got the job done so well. That’s why they offered the job in Washington DC to me. They recognized me, that we had a good organization, and we were getting the job done in Oregon and so they said, "We’d like to have you come to Washington and run the national base." So, that was a significant turning point, realizing that it was an opportunity. I remember a friend of mine -- oh. And then, I was offered a job in Washington as a deputy. Oh, no. I was interviewed to be the leader. They were interviewing three people for the leadership of the organization. I thought, "What are you asking me for? Little old me from Oregon, I don’t even have a doctorate. All I have is a bachelor’s." And they said, "Well, we’d like to be considered, like to consider you." So I said, "Okay." I went back for the interview. And I was, they took one of the other three. And so then, I thought, "Okay." Well, I knew the guy who got the job. And then, six months later he called me and said, "Say my deputy’s leaving. Will you come back as deputy?" My initial reaction was, "If you don’t want me for number one, you can’t have me for number two." No. A friend of mine said, "That’s ridiculous. You -- think all the good you can do at the national level and help the whole business, whatever." So I said, "Sure. I’ll come back." And so I did. And then a year and a half later, he left and there was another director. It was a very significant time, tremendously satisfying based on that story I told you and a whole pile of other things. And so, then a new political administration came in. Carter came in. And they changed the job I had which was the current professional to a political job and so, they kicked me out. And so, I talked to a friend of mine back there and he said, "Why don’t you apply for IPA, Intergovernmental Personnel Assignment?" which is a lot of apprentice people from any level of government, from city, county, state, national, to trade jobs, and any kind of arrangement. So, he said, "I bet you can become a professor out at the university, because of all your experience" or whatever. And so I said okay. I knew some people at Oregon State, I asked them if they’d take me on and I’d pay. It was a win-win situation. For them, I brought my salary, my money -- or my salary, my experience, everything. And they didn’t have to pay anything. It was free. And so I taught for four years and would ___+ students and whatever else. And so that was a significant turning point in my life. And then this Camp High Sierra program with the kids. It was wonderful then, of course. The time in Korea where I -- Oh. One of the other real turning points was when I got there, and I was a reserve. And the regulars, some of the regulars, felt that reserves were something less, incomplete, not very useful and some other things. And they had three rifle platoons at the company I was in, Howe Company. And they, and so I had the machine gun platoon and they divided the machine guns into squads and they wanted the platoons, so I didn’t have much to do. And then one of the platoon leaders got hurt and I should have gotten the job; but they gave it to a master sergeant who had been over there and been in combat. And I felt that I’d been mistreated. And afterwards I found out they had a new company commander who made that decision, afterwards. He and I became good friends and I said, "Why did you do that? I was the title of that, deserved it, and I didn’t get the chance at that time." And he said, "Well I talked to my, it was the company exec, and he said you’re a reserve, and don’t have enough experience, and whatever, so you shouldn’t get it." So he gave it to a sergeant. And I said, "Wait a minute. I’m an officer. I should have gotten it." Anyway, later, he said, "I apologize. That was a mistake. I shouldn’t have done it. It wasn’t fair to you." But then a little while later I got a platoon and did some things in combat. Interesting side issue, the fellow whose platoon I took over, he was a regular. He left in February of 1951, and I took over his rifle platoon on the hills of Korea. Said, "See ya." And then 27 years later, after my career and doing other things, I came back to Oregon. A friend of mine who had also been in Korea at the time in the Chosin Reservoir said, "Bob, why don’t we go to my friend’s house, and we’ll celebrate the Marine Corps birthday," which is a real tradition. And so, I did. And there was this guy. 27 years before, I said goodbye to him in the hills of Korea. And here he was in little old Corvalis. He was a, he was Lieutenant Colonel, and he was the assistant inspector instructor here on the ROTC program. Then he left, retired, went to Oregon, University of Oregon, and got a doctorate and became a national authority on mentally___ and disabled children. Still lives here. Anyway. So, Colonel Fredericks, his name is. Anyway, those are probably two or three of the real significant turning points. One other, one that’s kind of relative, when I had the battalion, or the reserves, where there was a captain who was up for promotion; and his company commander said that, told me he wasn’t going to promote or wasn’t going to give him a good ______report. Oh, and then shouldn’t, we should not give him the company because this fellow was, his tour was up and he was going to have to give up the company and he said don’t give it to the ‘exec, cause’ he can’t handle it. And I thought, "Doc, when I was in Korea, what happened to me when the sergeant got it instead of me?" And so I called the guy in and I said, "Now you know that your company commander says you shouldn’t get the job. But I’m getting ready for summer camp. I will give you the job. But you have to understand that if you do well, and this is the highlight of our year, two weeks of summer camp, if you do well, I’ll give you a fitness report that will get you a promotion. If you don’t, you have to get out of the reserve. That’s all." He had had 12 years. And so we agreed on everything he had to do. And when camp was over he said let’s talk. And he came and he said, "I didn’t do the job as well as I should have, so I’m going to resign." But the key was, he got the chance. I didn’t get that, initially. I later got it. Me and the company commander were good friends. We had a fine relationship. But all I wanted was a chance to perform. So that was a real important point to me. And, are you out of questions?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: You mentioned that your time in Korea was the most important. When you were over there, I imagine it was for at least a few months. What was the separation from your family like, and how did times did you have to depend --

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: I wasn’t married at the time, so it wasn’t a problem.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: But how was the relationship with the Marines that you worked with a significant part of your life?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Explain that a little differently. Phrase that a little differently.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: I imagine that you had to depend on your fellow Marines for support?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Over there.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: um-hum.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Oh, yeah. No question about it.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: The people who saved my life; and I, in turn, saved theirs in certain areas. So that’s one of the reasons, particularly when you’ve been in combat, you have the feeling "Once a Marine, always a Marine," cause’ you rely on them.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Sir, did you keep in touch with any of your friends from the Marine Corps?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Yeah. As a matter of fact, the company I was in was Howe Company, 3rd Battalion 5th Marines, H3-5. And that’s the company I was in, that’s when I had the platoon. And they kept that organization alive, and I still belong to it. And, we meet, they meet annually, and I was at the first one of them that I’ve attended, although this is about the 9th one. We had it, they had it in Medford and they have them all over the country._____ and to be a member, you have to have served at some time in Howe Company, 3rd Battalion, 5th Marines, all the way back from Guam, in World War II, to Vietnam and otherwise. And I went to one in Medford two years ago. And there were five people there who had been in my platoon when I was in Korea. Yeah. And that was 50’that’s what, 50 years. I hadn’t seen them in 50 years. INTERVIEWERS: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: And they, we miss it. That night it was, when I was, had the platoon, I went on patrol once on Valentine’s Day. 51’ we got ambushed. And we lost one of the people in the platoon, and a couple other people got hurt. And one of the guys says, "I remember you told me to get on the tank so we could get out of there." 50 years ago, you remember that (laughter)? So yeah, that answers your question. We had that relationship. And with this Colonel Fredericks, we together often, we play golf together. We have lunch fairly often, every couple weeks. And it’s a relationship that I treasure. That’s all. It’s just something for everyone. Anything else?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: (pause) Well, actually, I have one more question. Like, food’s a big part of my life. So, I was wondering what the food was like over there, like if you ate out of emeries?? or what you had.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: Well, in Korea we had, we were on sea rations at one time for 72 days. And so people had, I remember one person in our platoon had to go to the bathroom 21 times in one night (interviewers chuckling). Well, when you’re on the go frequently you couldn’t heat the food. You’d just eat it cold. And so, but, depending on where you are, if you’re not up in the front lines, they’d bring hot food to you. They have a canister. You’ve probably seen them when you’re training and things like that, about that high. And they bring out hot food. But other times you just have cold rations and that -- at one period of time, we just had cold rations for that one time.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: What is a sea ration? A Oh, they’re, they’re a combination, depending on -- this a long time ago. They, what they were, you get a box like this, with, depending on breakfast, lunch and dinner. Breakfast, you’d get a packet with cocoa. It looked like a big thick cookie of cocoa. And you get salt and pepper and a little package of cigarettes. And you’d have a can of scrambled eggs, pork and beans, chicken and rice, hamburgers, other things. And usually to heat those, you’d get little heat cabs and you’d put em’ in a can and heat them and then, they had a can opener, that’s what you eat. And a lot of times, you’d just eat them cold. You couldn’t heat it, or whatever. And then, you had canteen cups, so we, if we had water, you’d have water, you could make your chocolate. And you’d trade em’ around. Some people hated chicken and rice, so they’d trade two chicken and rice for one pork and beans, or whatever.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: So, it was that kind of thing. But other times, we’d, when we were back, after we came back from the Reservoir and we were down South, we were in tents, and hot chow every day and the trays, and that’s all, and it was different. So, it varied substantially depending on where you were and the conditions. But you get used to it. And if you looked at the person next to you and they’re getting’ used to it, you think, I can too. You just adopt that philosophy. We were miserable, I remember one time, we’d hiked about 20 miles in this miserable weather. And it was cold, almost freezing and mud. We had to dig a box hole, full a water bomb and starry-gaze it. I talked to one of the men the next morning after the miserable place we went that one time and slept. first time I didn’t sleep at night. And he said, "You know, I had the first experience of my life this morning. Last night, I thought I died, and this morning I woke up and thought I didn’t. (interviewers chuckling)" So that happens. Anything else?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: What was the adjustment like once you returned back from Korea and China?

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: It was difficult for a while, although I’m pretty flexible. People would say, "Where you been? I haven’t see ya for a while, Bob." And I’d say "Oh, I’ve been in Korea." "Korea. What’re you doing in Korea? What’s happening there?" That kind of thing. It was, I couldn’t believe it, And a number of other people that I get apprehensive about. They didn’t even know what we were doing over there in Korea. I saw more people that I thought, maybe didn’t know either but anyway that was a situation that was, we had to adjust to it. Okay. So you didn’t know about it but somebody had to be there. I was there, and that was it.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Sir, do you feel that you had the support of the general public more than people not supporting you? Because now, sometimes these days, we’ll walk through campus in our uniforms, and there will be people protesting, and they’ll openly protest against us and --

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: I don’t think the people supported us at the time like they would at war after World War II. After World War II, "Great, you were wonderful, veterans, and you saved our butts, and glad you were there, and thanks." But it wasn’t like that way with Korea. We got an ambushed even worse because I wasn’t involved with them. But yeah, it was disappointing, that the people didn’t really know about it or care about it, but, whatever. The satisfaction we had, at least I had, was, I was there. It had to be done. I was the one who was trying to do it, did the best I could, and I think we did a good job.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Well, sir, we have a couple forms for you to fill out, but I wanted to say thank you so much for spending your time explaining this all to us. You’ve done an excellent job. So thank you.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: You’re welcome.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Thank you, sir.

sp.speaker: Robert W. Schoning
sp.p: You’re welcome.
